stories.headline: Champions League: Bellingham wondergoal helps Real Madrid thump PSV; Arsenal and Man City held
stories.deck: Mbappe scores twice in Madrid’s 5-1 rout; Arsenal were held 1-1 at home by Borussia Dortmund and Manchester City drew ​2-2 with Napoli
stories.bodyText:
Jude Bellingham came off the bench to score a spectacular goal as Real Madrid maintained their perfect Champions League start with a 5-1 comeback victory over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday (November 24, 2026), while ‌Arsenal were held 1-1 at home by Borussia Dortmund and Manchester City drew 2-2 with Napoli.
Real Madrid looked in real trouble at home to PSV, going in at the break behind to Ivan Perisic's penalty, before they roared back through a goal from Federico Valverde and Bellingham's stunning strike.
Having seen an acrobatic volley blocked minutes earlier, the England midfielder controlled Kylian Mbappe's pass with two ‌touches in the air and curled a superb shot into the far corner from well outside the area.
Mbappe netted twice to put Real out of sight before Vinicius Jr ‌got in on the act with a late goal having struck the post twice earlier ‌in the game.
Real moved top of the standings on 15 points, three ahead of Paris St Germain who host AS Roma on Wednesday. Como, 1-0 winners over AEK Athens, and Real Betis, who beat Slovan Bratislava 2-0, also have 12 points, one more than Arsenal.
The Premier League leaders' clash with their Bundesliga counterparts ended all square after a second-half goal from Dortmund's Maximilian Beier ‌cancelled out Viktor Gyokeres' strike in the 10th minute.
Manchester City had to come from behind twice after a scoreless opening half. Ayyoub Bouaddi equalised following Rasmus Hojlund's opener for Napoli and Rayan Cherki scored four minutes from time to rescue a point for City after Noa Lang ‌put Napoli back in front.
Bellingham beauty
Jose Mourinho won the Champions League with Porto and Inter Milan, but fell at the semi-final stage in each of his three seasons during his previous spell in charge at Real. He opted to leave Bellingham on the bench for the visit of PSV, and it almost went horribly wrong.
PSV took a deserved lead in the 32nd minute, with 37-year-old captain Perisic showing all his experience, ignoring the whistles ringing out around the ‌Bernabeu before sending Thibaut Courtois the wrong way from the spot.
They almost doubled their lead before the break as the unmarked Kodai Sano glanced a header off target as the visitors continued to cause Real serious problems.
Mourinho responded with three changes at the interval, including the introduction of Bellingham.
"We were struggling to keep possession but, when Jude came on, he gave us that peace of mind and we could play much better," Valverde told Movistar.
Real equalised five minutes after the break, thanks to Arda ‌Guler's quick-thinking, with the Turkish midfielder flicking a backheeled pass to Valverde in the area, who steered his first-time shot into the bottom corner.
Real's fans were on their feet 10 minutes later, scarcely believing what they had seen, while Bellingham's teammates looked similarly shell-shocked.
Marc Cucurella walked away with his head in his hands in wonder while the other Real players rushed to congratulate the scorer.
Real took command after Bellingham's goal and punished a loose pass in the PSV defence, Guler finding the unmarked Mbappe to extend the France forward's scoring run to seven successive Champions League ‌appearances.
Mbappe added his second before Vinicius rounded off a resounding victory from Bellingham's pass, underlining the Spanish side's credentials as serious contenders to take PSG's crown.
Elsewhere, Porto claimed a 1-0 win at Feyenoord, RB Leipzig defeated Lens 3-1, Galatasaray beat Aston Villa 1-0 and Bodo/Glimt beat LASK by the same scoreline.

stories.headline: World Chess Championship: Gukesh says preparation tougher than playing
stories.deck: The Indian, playing with the black pieces, will have the advantage of white in Wednesday's (November 25, 2026) second game
stories.bodyText:
Playing the game is "the easiest thing" while the real work lies in preparation, said defending champion D Gukesh after overcoming "a little scary" time pressure to open his World Championship title defence with a draw against Javokhir Sindarov.
Playing with black, Gukesh was put under severe time pressure by Sindarov in a game that lasted 38 moves. But the Indian ace survived the testing moments to split the point, with the game ending 0.5-0.5.
The Indian, playing with the black pieces, will have the advantage of white in Wednesday's (November 25, 2026) second game, having safely negotiated the opening challenge against an opponent widely regarded as a favourite based on rating and recent form.
"It looked equal the whole time, some problems to solve but I think both of us played a very good game," Gukesh said during the post-game interaction.
The defending champion admitted that the opening presented a few challenges and required him to take his time, though the clock situation briefly caused some concern.
"The pressure on the clock was looking a little scary but should be fine," he said.
Asked about his overall experience of the opening game, Gukesh said: "This is the easiest thing, to go and play the game. Before that there is so much work to do, but when u get there, you know you are home."
Sindarov, meanwhile, felt he had managed to put Gukesh under some pressure but acknowledged that the Indian defended accurately.
"I got some pressure and I was pushing but he found a very good defense. I was trying to push every moment because of the clock, but in the end he found the best moves," he said.
The attention surrounding the contest, which features the youngest-ever World Championship match-up between two players in their twenties, has also brought considerable scrutiny.
Sindarov, however, said he was trying not to let the occasion affect his approach.
"I know that the whole chess world is watching this match, normally it’s a big pressure but I am trying not to think about this. I am just trying to adapt to the atmosphere in the playing hall, the first thing is to play good chess," he said.
Gukesh echoed his opponent's sentiments, saying adapting to the conditions and focusing on performance were essential for any sportsperson.
"I don’t think one consciously thinks about these things, as a sports person you just need to adapt to different conditions and find a way to perform at your best," he said.
The players will have two more games over the next two days before the first rest day. Thereafter, a rest day will follow every three games.
With the opening encounter ending in a draw, the contest remains evenly poised, but Gukesh will look to make the most of his first outing with the white pieces in the second game.

stories.headline: Passenger on moving bike takes one-handed catch in Pakistan; video goes viral
stories.deck: The catch came in the sixth over of GKR Dir's innings when a batter struck the ball over the extra-cover boundary.
stories.bodyText:
A passenger on a moving motorcycle caught a ball hit for six outside the stadium during a Swat Premier League match between Swat Strikers and GKR Dir in Pakistan. The incident took place during the tournament's eighth season and has since gone viral on social media.
The catch came in the sixth over of GKR Dir's innings when a batter struck the ball over the extra-cover boundary. The shot cleared the stadium and travelled outside the ground, where a passenger sitting on a passing motorcycle managed to catch it with one hand while the vehicle was still moving.
The video has attracted attention on social media, with users reacting to the catch and comparing it with some of the fielding efforts seen in international cricket. One user described it as the "Catch of the century". Another appeared to refer to New Zealand's Glenn Phillips, who is known for taking difficult catches on the field, and wrote, "Phillips who?"
The Swat Premier League is a local tape-ball tournament in Pakistan, with each team getting 10 overs to bat in an innings. The incident happened during Match 4 of the competition between Swat Strikers and GKR Dir.
While the catch outside the stadium became the talking point, Swat Strikers also secured a 34-run win in the match. They posted 148/6 in their allotted 10 overs before restricting GKR Dir to 114/9, sealing the victory.
The viral moment has added an unusual talking point to a match that otherwise saw Swat Strikers dominate the contest.

stories.headline: Selector must have stature, not just a seat at the table: Dilip Vengsarkar
stories.deck: Former India captain and chief selector says travelling selector should be a strong, neutral voice in picking XI and must ‘put his foot down’ when something is blatantly wrong.
stories.bodyText:
At a time when India’s team selection has come under scrutiny following the controversial calls involving 
Mohammed Siraj
 and 
Ravindra Jadeja
 in Wellington, former India captain and chief selector 
Dilip Vengsarkar
 believes the solution lies not merely in having a selector travel with the team, but in ensuring that the men doing the job have the stature to challenge the captain and coach.
Vengsarkar, widely regarded as one of India’s finest chairmen of selectors, feels the travelling selector cannot simply be an observer. He should be part of the process of choosing the playing XI and, crucially, be strong enough to intervene when he believes the team management is getting a major call wrong.
“When I was chairman of the selection committee, if any member of the five-man committee went on a tour, he would chair the selection meeting along with the captain and vice-captain. The meeting would be convened by the manager,” Vengsarkar told TOI.
“So, automatically, the selector chairing the meeting had a say in the playing XI. The meeting should involve the selector, coach, captain and vice-captain and be convened by the manager,” he stated.
With Shubman Gill still inexperienced in his job as Test captain, should the selection committee then carry greater responsibility over what XI plays?
Vengsarkar believes the captain’s age or experience is not necessarily the issue here.
“It depends on the stature of the person who is the selector there on tour. If a person without stature accompanies the team, he can be influenced or dominated,” he said.
During Vengsarkar’s stint as chief selector, his panel included Venkatapathy Raju, Ranjib Biswal, Bhupinder Singh Sr and Sanjay Jagdale. Vengsarkar says he and Jagdale chaired selection meetings when they travelled with the team.
He recalled an episode from a tour which, without naming the captain or coach involved, illustrated why a strong selector could become an important balancing presence.
“The coach told me to sort things out because he felt slighted as the captain was not consulting him at all while picking the XI. I sat beside the captain and told him, ‘I will chair the meeting, along with you and the vice-captain, and let the manager convene it.’ The captain immediately agreed and said, ‘If you are chairing the meeting, I have no issues.’”
For Vengsarkar, the danger in leaving the playing XI entirely to the captain and coach is that the two are always closely aligned. That can leave little room for a dissenting view. “If you give the power to pick the XI only to the coach and captain, they generally are always on the same page. That gives them room to bring in their personal likes and dislikes. Let the selector on tour be the neutral voice. If it is a 50-50 call, the selector should always go with the captain. But if you spot something blatantly wrong, he must put his foot down.”
Vengsarkar insists this is not an issue restricted to the present set-up. Previous captain-coach combinations, he says, have also enjoyed unhinged power.
Without identifying players, he recalled how a cricketer who had scored heavily in an important tournament was relegated to 12th-man duties in the next series because he was viewed as competition for the captain. He cited another instance of a Test cricketer who stood in as captain, won an important Test and soon found himself on the bench. “I would not have allowed it,” he says.
As India captain, Vengsarkar did not have the luxury of touring selectors, not least because the BCCI did not have its present financial muscle. “Especially when a series was happening in the West Indies, selectors would not travel. I would ask my vice-captain and another senior player to sit in the meeting along with the manager,” he recalled.
His tenure as chief selector also showed that a robust selection structure need not mean confrontation between selector and captain. “There were a lot of questions around Virender Sehwag’s selection for the 2007-08 Australia tour. He had not been part of the England tour earlier that year. But Anil Kumble and I were on the same page and we picked him as the 17th member, despite another opener having scored more runs than him in domestic cricket,” Vengsarkar said.
Ultimately, Vengsarkar believes the quality and independence of the individual matter more than merely putting a selector on the plane. “It has become such a lucrative job that sometimes many prefer to stay quiet, take their package and avoid rocking the boat with the coach, captain or board when it comes to selecting or dropping players.”

briefs.headline: IND vs NZ Test series: No point reading the pitch too much, says Matt Henry
briefs.deck: Henry, who has enjoyed considerable success at his home ground, said New Zealand would prepare for different possibilities rather than make assumptions based on the venue's traditional characteristics
briefs.bodyText:
Senior New Zealand pacer Matt Henry does not want to read too much into the nature of the Hagley Oval surface ahead of the second Test against India in Christchurch after the opening game's track in Wellington ended up being a batting paradise despite its reputation of being a seamer-friendly pitch.
Henry, who has enjoyed considerable success at his home ground, said New Zealand would prepare for different possibilities rather than make assumptions based on the venue's traditional characteristics.
Only 24 wickets fell in the drawn first game across five days with India pulling off their biggest overseas total of 720. Visiting skipper Shubman Gill said he was very disappointed with the placid track after the two teams shook hands with more than 15 overs left to be bowled on the final day.
"I think every game's different, every surface you play on is slightly different as well. And I think there's been a lot of runs scored here of late as well," Henry said at a press conference on Wednesday.
"So for us, it's probably not to get carried away with what it could be and trying to read pitches. It's a pretty fine art to do that."
The second Test gets underway on Friday.
The batting-friendly nature of the venue was evident during India A's four-day match against New Zealand A here earlier this month, when the contest ended in a draw after a glut of runs.
New Zealand A scored 424 riding on Matt Boyle's 110 after India A scored 346 in their first innings courtesy Dhruv Jurel's 105.
India A then piled up 282 for two in their second innings, with Yashasvi Jaiswal remaining unbeaten on 155. The pitch had completely flattened out by then.
Henry acknowledged that Hagley Oval has traditionally offered assistance to fast bowlers, particularly when there is bounce and carry, but said the surface can become increasingly favourable for batting as the match progresses.
"I think traditionally here in New Zealand, the wickets when there's grass on them tend to get better and better, and it's been the same here. It's a good batting venue. Obviously, when there's bounce involved, it's good for the bowler, but from a batting point of view you can score runs quickly as well," he said.
However, Henry had a word of caution for batters -- they would need to trust their defense a lot more.
"There's moments where you probably have to rely on your defence a little bit, but when you get through those periods, you really can put bowlers under pressure because, like you said, when it flattens out, your margins become pretty small as a bowler."
The 34-year-old said the experience of playing at the venue over the years gives the home team a certain degree of comfort, although it would still need to assess the conditions as the match unfolds.
"It's always nice when you're at home and it is a ground you've played a lot of cricket at, so you probably have that element of comfort. You kind of know the ground well and whatnot.
"But yeah, it's been a great place to play cricket in the past, somewhere I love to play cricket.
Henry also backed Jacob Duffy, who endured an expensive outing in the drawn opening Test, conceding more than 200 runs, saying the pacer was willing to embrace different plans in the team's interest rather than worry about his individual figures.
"He's (Duffy) shown over the years what a classy bowler he is. He's all about the team, so when we suggest maybe we do a bumper plan here, he's not worried about his personal figures.
"He's trying to have an impact on the game and the moments that required him to probably be more attacking on quite a docile wicket," Henry said to a query from PTI.
"For him to just buy into that team-first mentality is so impressive. There's no question about the skill. For us, there were moments when we needed someone to try a different plan, and he was open to do that."
Henry said Duffy's willingness to adapt reflected the team's collective approach, particularly on surfaces where conventional bowling methods might not yield results.
"It's not worrying about the outcome but how you're trying to have an impact on the game.
The impacts he's had over the last few years have been match-winning impacts because of his mindset.
"We're not too worried whatsoever. I think it's more about what he's bringing to the table. He's nothing but a team man and doing great stuff for us, and I'm sure that will continue to be the case." PTI KHS PM PM

briefs.headline: Sooryavanshi makes history with a 52-ball double ton — but tougher tests await
briefs.deck: At 15, Sooryavanshi rewrites List A history with a 52-ball double ton. But the real test lies ahead, against stronger attacks.
briefs.bodyText:
When it’s Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, records keep falling like nine-pins. On Tuesday, on a nondescript ground in Doha, it was the turn of United Arab Emirates to face his wrath in the Rising Stars Asia Cup as the 15-year-old smashed an astonishing 53-ball 204 that took India ‘A’ to the semifinals.
His 52-ball 200 included a hundred off 28 balls — another List A record — as India chased down 250 in a ridiculous 14.2 overs, with senior batters like Prabhsimran Singh and Rinku Singh at the other end only left to applaud the effort.
Current-day cricket’s fan isn’t a stranger to this kind of carnage from Vaibhav’s bat. Standing tall and holding his shape, he smashed the UAE bowlers with absolute disdain — 28 sixes raining from his willow, the highest in an innings in any format!
“I didn’t score in the first two games. After assessing the wicket, I thought there was not much for bowlers so I decided to back my game. Mindset was the same as every game, I wanted to bat long,” Sooryavanshi told the host broadcaster after the win.
While Sooryavanshi broke Australia’s Jake Fraser-McGurk’s fastest List A hundred by one ball, he comfortably surpassed Chad Bowes’ 103-ball double for Canterbury.
Sooryavanshi’s ability to generate easy power and smash sixes at will had earned him a call in the India U-19 side as a 13-year-old. Ranadeb Bose, one of the members of the junior national selection committee which chose the chubby-cheeked boy for the first time in 2022, told TOI how they first saw the left-hander in a game which they were not supposed to cover.
“It was the Vinoo Mankad event in 2022 and we were supposed to be at another ground. But that ground was not ready due to overnight rain and that’s why we went to see this Bihar boy whom we had heard about. And what an experience that was!” Bose said.
Sooryavanshi’s ability to keep a completely uncluttered mind and simply react to the ball was stand-out for Bose.
“The way he played the short ball as a 13-year-old was unbelievable. We immediately knew that this is a jewel who needs to be nurtured,” the former selector said.
The selectors were tempted to include him for the U-19 World Cup team in South Africa in 2024, but decided against it. “The 
BCCI
 has a rule that no player can play more than one U-19 World Cup. And, that’s a great rule. (Because) We wanted to hold him back for a couple of more years,” Bose added.
But Vaibhav didn’t wait for the U-19 World Cup to make his mark. Picked by 
Rajasthan Royals
, he was a smash hit in the 
IPL
 and went on to play for India. “Early this year, we played him in the U-19 World Cup. Till the final, he had an indifferent tournament. But the beauty of Vaibhav is he is never under any kind of pressure ... He went into the England final as if it’s just another game and smashed that matchwinning 175,” Bose said.
Sooryavanshi has gone from strength to strength over the years and now he is a regular member of the senior Indian squad, though a spot in the XI isn’t guaranteed. India head coach 
Gautam Gambhir has maintained that he will have to wait for his chance as players like Sanju Samson and Ishan Kishan ahead of him.
Bose, too, is on the same page with Gambhir. The former Bengal pacer feels that even though the Tuesday effort was stupendous, it will be important for Sooryavanshi to come good in the more crucial games. “This UAE attack is, at best, a mid-level Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy attack and Vaibhav has crossed this stage. I want him to do this against Pakistan, which has a good bowling attack. If he does that, we’ll know he is really ready,” the former Bengal paceman said.
Sooryavanshi, too, will be equally keen to rise to the occasion, if he gets the chance this Sunday.

briefs.headline: The Brar decision: India stare at big pace-bowling call with WTC hopes on the line
briefs.deck: India face a selection dilemma in Christchurch, with Gurnoor Brar's extra pace and ability to bowl long spells potentially offering a solution to their struggles on flat surfaces. With WTC points at stake and a draw not enough, the team management could be forced to rethink its pace combination ahead of the second Test.
briefs.bodyText:
CHRISTCHURCH: With just a three-day turnaround between the two Tests, India cancelled their practice session on November 25. Collectively, the fast bowlers sent down 182 overs in the series opener, so balancing the need to keep their bodies fresh is hardly surprising. Shubman Gill & Co. are set to train on the eve of the match and will hold another selection huddle ahead of the second Test, starting Friday.
Tuesday was a rather unusual day, even for the locals, which kept the city centre buzzing. The Indian cricketers didn't waste a moment after checking into their city hotel, heading out in different groups to grab a quick bite near the team hotel. The sun was out and the breeze was gentle enough to keep the caps in place. The locals, however, had a word of caution, suggesting a wild week ahead.
"You never know with Christchurch. It is not as windy as Wellington, but the forecast can surprise you. It can be a bit wild, so keep checking the app," says a staff member at a popular Indian restaurant. "Do keep the umbrellas handy," she adds with a chuckle.
Although rain is forecast on some days, conditions currently look largely pleasant, with temperatures hovering in the 20s. 
Unlike Wellington, there are no wild spells of wind here. Most of India's Test players are very well accustomed to this city, having spent a lot of time here when the A team played three fixtures preceding the Tests.
From 
Jasprit Bumrah
 to 
Yashasvi Jaiswal
, as many as 13 squad members have had game time here, and seven of them played the second A game at Hagley Oval. It was a high-scoring fixture where Jaiswal and Dhruv Jurel scored tons, and it followed a pattern similar to Wellington: early wickets followed by a struggle once the ball got old.
The scenario is likely to be discussed when the captain and coach firm up their plans for the second game. Even though Gill lauded the current group for their energy and body language on a flat pitch, Gurnoor Brar will be back in the discussion for his extra pace and ability to bowl long spells without losing pace.
The fast bowler from Punjab was very close to making his debut in Colombo, but the think tank persisted with the experience of Siraj. The move backfired, and it will be interesting to see whether they are adventurous enough to tweak the quartet of Bumrah, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj. It could sound like a harsh call or a knee-jerk reaction, but India need to assemble an attack capable of making inroads even when there is nothing on offer.
 And that could well be the case in Christchurch too.
No matter how much grass the curator leaves on the pitch, if the conditions overhead are not supportive, a Basin-like blockathon could well return to the menu. Prasidh was very underwhelming in the first innings of the first Test but found his rhythm in the second and looked the most effective bowler. Akash set up the game nicely in the first innings, and Kamboj did his job with both bat and ball.
So who goes out if Brar comes in? A tricky call awaits the management as they chase crucial World Test Championship points. A draw won't suffice for a team pressing for a final berth, and an unfavourable result this week could well draw curtains on their slim hopes. For a side emphasising current form over reputation, it will be interesting to see how the selection plays out over the next couple of days.

briefs.headline: Ben Stokes enters IPL auction at maximum base price; 11 Bangladesh players in pool
briefs.deck: Stokes, who retired from international cricket earlier this year, last featured in the IPL in 2023, when he played two matches for Chennai Super Kings. He has also represented Rajasthan Royals and the now-defunct Rising Pune Supergiant.
briefs.bodyText:
Former England captain 
Ben Stokes
 and Australian batter 
Cameron Bancroft
 are among the overseas players who have registered for the IPL auction, news agency PTI reported. The auction is scheduled to take place in Goa on December 16.
Stokes, who retired from international cricket earlier this year, has set his base price at Rs 2 crore. The all-rounder last played in the IPL in 2023, turning out for 
Chennai Super Kings
 in two matches. He has also represented Rajasthan Royals and the now-defunct Rising Pune Supergiant.
Bancroft, who has been in the news following fresh revelations about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, has registered at a base price of Rs 75 lakh. He has never played in the IPL but regularly features in the Big Bash League (BBL).
Another Australian, fast bowler Scott Boland, has also entered the auction. However, he is not expected to be available for most of the tournament.
No Mustafizur, but 11 Bangladesh players register for IPL auction
As many as 11 Bangladesh players have registered for the auction, but fast bowler Mustafizur Rahman is not among them. Rahman was released by Kolkata Knight Riders on the BCCI's instructions last year. 
The development eventually led to Bangladesh withdrawing from the T20 World Cup in India.
The Bangladesh players in the auction register are Hasan Mahmud, Parvez Hossain Emon, Ripon Mondol, Rishad Hossain, Saif Hassan, Shak Mahedi Hasan, Shamim Hossain, Shoriful Islam, Tanzim Hasan Sakib, Towhid Hridoy and Md Rubel.
Japan's Benjamin Ito Davis is among the players from associate nations who could go under the hammer in Goa. He has a base price of Rs 30 lakh.
A total of 1,220 players have registered for the auction, including 939 Indians and 281 overseas players. The 10 franchises have a maximum of 66 slots to fill, of which 25 are reserved for overseas players. The list is expected to be cut down significantly before the auction.

briefs.headline: World Chess C'ship Round 1: How Gukesh won in 38-move draw over Sindarov
briefs.deck: Gukesh drew his opening 38-move World Championship game against Javokhir Sindarov despite facing severe time pressure and an aggressive opening attack. Playing with black, he showed excellent defensive skills, neutralised Sindarov’s advantage and escaped danger without major mistakes. Although the match ended level, Gukesh gained a psychological victory, boosting his confidence ahead of Game 2.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: "Sindarov has a 60 min advantage over Gukesh. What did Gukesh’s team do all this time for the last 2 years?" A random post on X was enough to gauge the tension in the air as two 20-year-old prodigies, Javokhir Sindarov and Dommaraju Gukesh, locked horns in a taut, high-wire curtain-raiser at the 2026 World Chess Championship in Cologny, Switzerland.
Minutes later, another screenshot made the rounds. It was not fake or AI-generated. By move 17, the reigning world champion, with Black, was staring at a dwindling 29:51 on his clock, while his Uzbek challenger sat comfortably behind a fortress of over an hour and eighteen minutes.
Before move 40, there is no increment, and the math seemed brutal as the titleholder was already staring down the barrel of severe time trouble.
Blitzing through the opening stages to turn the clock into a weapon has become Sindarov’s calling card. Earlier this year in Cyprus, wielding the very same high-tempo blueprint, the Uzbek grandmaster tore through the Candidates field like a whirlwind.
On Tuesday, playing with the white pieces, which gives the first-move advantage, he looked poised to run that exact playbook once again.
Asked afterwards about the ticking clock, Gukesh replied, "I thought I was always under control, or at least not in a place where I really needed to be worried... I was happy that I managed to spend some time and find a good solution (to the opening problems)!"
How the game unfolded
The battle took place in a famous chess setup known as the Berlin Endgame, a notoriously solid, defensive strategy where the queens are traded off early.
While it is usually a safe choice, Gukesh rarely plays it, which raised eyebrows.
Sindarov wasted no time taking the game into uncharted territory, playing a surprise knight move on turn 13 (13. Ne4) that had never been seen in a top-level in-person tournament before.
As Dutch Grandmaster Anish Giri noted in his post-game breakdown, the players skipped the usual middle part of a chess game entirely, jumping straight into a tense, high-stakes endgame.
"White has a lot of initiative... very dangerous position for Black," Giri said on his YouTube channel.
Sindarov's pieces were swarming forward, while one of Gukesh's most powerful pieces, his rook in the corner, remained trapped and unable to join the fight.
Forced onto the back foot and burning precious minutes to calculate every danger, Gukesh found a clever defensive setup on moves 17 and 18 (17...Bb4 and 18...h6).
By pinning Sindarov’s pieces in place and blocking his path forward, the Indian champion brought White’s attack to a grinding halt.
Sindarov still held a slight edge and could have kept building the pressure slowly. Instead, on move 24, he pushed a pawn forward aggressively (24. f4), triggering a fast trade of pieces that accidentally gave Gukesh the escape route he needed.
Gukesh responded with cold-blooded accuracy, giving up a pawn to free his king and finally bring his trapped corner rook into the action.
"All Black's other pieces are good, but the rook on h8 is not in the game," Giri observed. "As soon as the king was able to move up and connect these rooks, bring this rook into play... the opening was essentially over."
Once Gukesh’s army was working together, the danger disappeared.
In fact, Sindarov had to make one very careful defensive move late in the game to avoid falling into a trap, before forcing a draw by repeating the same moves three times, a standard way chess games end in a tie when neither side can make progress.
Neither player made a single major mistake across all 38 moves.
Praise from top Grandmasters
The high-wire accuracy drew immediate acclaim from fellow grandmasters on X.
Grandmaster Srinath Narayanan wrote: "High quality game one, fitting of a world championship match. Love the amount of watching and interest, again fitting of a world championship match!"
Grandmaster Rameshbabu Praggnanandhaa posted, "Incredible 1st game of World Championship match! High quality game from both! Gukesh found great moves under pressure! Excited to follow game 2"
Grandmaster Vidit Gujrathi also joined in, adding, "A very high quality game considering the pressure of an opening round match. Sindarov showed a new opening idea but Gukesh found good moves, although he was dangerously low on time at some point. There was a lot of tension throughout the game, so very interesting to watch as a fan of the game."
While the scoreboard reads half-a-point apiece after a remarkably clean opener, it is Gukesh who will rest easier in Cologny tonight, having survived an early storm with the defensive black pieces before getting the attacking white pieces in Game 2.
On the FIDE broadcast, commentator Grandmaster 
Peter Leko
 summed up perfectly, "We should say that Gukesh is the winner of the game psychologically because playing with the black pieces, he got under pressure, but he navigated all the difficulties, knowing that he had a rough year, facing a challenge in the very first game, and being uncomfortable not being able to show his prep, and then played the way he did. I think this is the boost he needed."

briefs.headline: Sooryavanshi breaks AB de Villiers' long-standing record with historic 204 off 53
briefs.deck: In a stunning cricket display, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi shattered records by smashing 204 runs off just 53 balls, showcasing his skill with seven fours and an astonishing 28 sixes. India A completed a remarkable chase of 250 runs in only 14.2 overs, securing victory by seven wickets. UAE's Harpreet Singh Bhatia contributed significantly with 130 runs, helping his team reach a total of 249.
briefs.bodyText:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scripted another slice of cricket history with his sensational 204 off just 53 balls against the UAE in the ACC Men's Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026 on Tuesday. The India A opener registered a staggering strike rate of 384.90, surpassing the long-standing record held by former South Africa captain AB de Villiers for the highest strike rate in a List A innings featuring a century.
De Villiers had held the record since January 2015, when he smashed 149 off just 44 deliveries against the West Indies in Johannesburg at a strike rate of 338.63. Australia's Jake Fraser-McGurk occupied the third spot with his 125 off 38 balls at a strike rate of 328.94 for South Australia against Tasmania in 2023.
Sooryavanshi's remarkable knock featured seven fours and 28 sixes. He brought up his century in just 28 balls before completing his double century in 53 deliveries, producing one of the most destructive innings in List A cricket.
His extraordinary batting display also powered India A to a dominant seven-wicket victory. Chasing 250, India A reached 254/3 in just 14.2 overs, turning the contest into a one-sided affair.
Highest strike rates in List A centuries
India A thrash UAE  by seven-wickets
India A registered a stunning seven-wicket victory over UAE in their Rising Stars Asia Cup clash, chasing down a target of 250 in just 14.2 overs. UAE had posted 249/8 in their 50 overs, with 
Harpreet Singh Bhatia
 leading the innings with a brilliant 130 off 144 balls, including 12 fours and four sixes. 
Basil Hameed also chipped in with an unbeaten 36 off 36 deliveries, while Arshad Khan was the pick of the Indian bowlers, claiming four wickets for 43 runs.
However, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi completely took the game away from UAE with a breathtaking 204 off just 53 balls. The youngster smashed seven fours and a record-breaking 28 sixes, reaching his century in just 28 deliveries before completing his double century off 53 balls. His extraordinary assault powered India A to 254/3 in only 14.2 overs, with 
Rinku Singh
 remaining unbeaten on 21.

briefs.headline: World chess championship: Gritty Gukesh weathers time pressure, holds Sindarov
briefs.deck: The defending champion, who was battling the clock for most of the opening game, manages to salvage a draw
briefs.bodyText:

The computer had white pieces and it opted for the Spanish Game. Anand, who hadn’t yet won any of his World titles yet, played the Berlin Defence. It is a solid option when you are playing with black pieces.
And it was Berlin Defence that D. Gukesh opted for the opening game of his World chess championship match against Javokhir Sindarov in Geneva on Tuesday.
The chess world had indeed been curious about the opening in the first game of the widely anticipated match between the 20-year-olds.
Sindarov began by pushing the pawn in front of him by two squares, to which Gukesh replied with a similar move. Just seven moves later, the queens were off the board, and a draw would become the likeliest result later on.
And it was draw. But it wasn’t a tame, dull peace treaty.
There were some anxious moves along the way, and there was also a battle on the clock, which Gukesh was losing for most of the time.
There were several periods when it seemed he could get into serious time trouble that could cost him dear. At one stage, he had to make his 22 moves in 24 minutes.
Sindarov, at that stage, was very comfortably placed. And then, Gukesh had some six minutes for nine moves.
The Chennai Grandmaster was indeed struggling. He, however, kept his calm, even as the game continued on even terms more or less.
Later on, Sindarov was also forced to take more time to make his moves. He had been blitzing away earlier, and had enough time to move about inside the Fondation Martin Bodmer, the famous library in Cologny, the venue of the match.
The first game, featuring a same-coloured-bishop ending, was eventually drawn by a repetition of moves, of which 38 were played in all. It was a game worthy of a World championship match.
Gukesh later said that he thought he was always under control.
“It wasn’t in a place where I really needed to be worried,” he said.
Sindarov said he was trying to push at every moment because of the advantage on the clock. “But Gukesh defended well in the end,” he said.
